To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the strategic decision-making literature is divided into two camps, the procedural rationality and the political behavior camps, and (2) these two dimensions are not related to one another.

(1) the political and rational dimensions of the strategic-decision-making process are independent; (2) rationality is more important than politics in strategic decision making; (3) rationality is a more powerful predictor of strategic-decision outcomes than politics; and (4) rationality is the only significant predictor of the quality of the strategic decision.

(1) procedural rationality and the use of political behavior are two independent and separate dimensions of the strategic management process, and (2) managers use both rational and political approaches to make strategic decisions, but they tend to use one or the other.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the strategic decision-making processes used by managers in organizations to make decisions.
the strategic decision-making processes that occur within organizations.
the relationship between rationality and political processes in strategic decision making.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are two types of decision-making behavior in organizations: rational and political.
rationality and political behaviors are independent dimensions of strategic decision making.
the political process is not the only way of making strategic decisions, nor are all strategic decisions made in this way.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the strategic decision-making literature has been dominated by two distinct perspectives, rationality and politics.
political behavior is a separate, but not necessarily competing dimension of the decision-making process.
strategic decisions are made in a political context.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the rationality of strategic decision making is a separate dimension from the political behavior of decision makers.
the rationality of the decision-making process is not a function of the political behavior that occurs during the decision-making process.
managers can use rational and political approaches to decision making, and that these approaches are complementary rather than competing.
